newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Reuters poll finds blue-chip firms upbeat on HK.
newsitem.headline: Reuters poll finds blue-chip firms upbeat on HK.

text.p: Hong Kong's top companies are overwhelmingly positive about the territory's business outlook in the year after Hong Kong reverts to China and for several years afterwards, a Reuters survey shows.

Of 11 blue-chip companies asked, all said they were positive about Hong Kong's business environment in the next year. Ten said they were positive about the outlook over five years, while just one company said it was not positive.

"Hong Kong will remain an attractive place to do business given its excellent infrastructure as well as its low tax rate and its advantageous location close to China," Cathay Pacific Airways Ltd wrote in response to the query.
Hong Kong reverts to China at midnight on June 30 after more than 150 years of British colonial rule.
Five respondents forecast that Hong Kong's economy would grow faster over the next five years, while five saw growth advancing at roughly current levels and one predicted a slowing of the economy.
The Hong Kong government estimates the economy advanced at a 4.7 percent clip in 1996 and has forecast a growth rate of 5.5 percent for 1997.

Asked about their business plans, seven of the blue-chip companies said they expect their business to expand in the next year, while four expect their operations to be maintained at roughly current levels. None expect business to contract.
Over five years, 10 expect their businesses to expand while one foresees a contraction.

Hongkong and Shanghai Hotels Ltd, which declined to participate in the survey, nevertheless noted it has devoted additional resources to Hong Kong through the redevelopment of its flagship, the Peninsula Hotel, and the new Peak Tower.
"Investment of this order in itself is a tangible vote of confidence not only in the present but also in the future of Hong Kong," a company spokeswoman said.
One property developer was blunt about its positive outlook.
"No alternative," the company said in answer to the survey.

All of the companies surveyed do business with China. Six of the firms see their China operations expanding over the next year, while four see China business staying roughly the same and one foresees a contraction.
Over the next five years, the view was unanimous -- all expect to be doing more business with China.
All of the respondents said they expect Hong Kong to remain the main conduit for investment in China over the next five years.
Only two of the respondents said plans to weaken civil liberties in Hong Kong would adversely affect their confidence in Hong Kong's future as a business and financial centre.
Eight said the watering down of rights would have no effect on business, while one of the survey respondents did not answer the question on rights.

Last Thursday, the office of post-handover leader Tung Chee-hwa unveiled a diluted version of restrictions on demonstrations and a modified ban on foreign funding of local political groups in response to criticism that the laws originally proposed were too harsh.
Several companies contacted by Reuters declined to air their views on the business outlook for Hong Kong.
